newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate rises to 5 percent in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate rises to 5 percent in June.

text.p: The unemployment rate jumped to 5 percent last month from a 24-year low 4.8 percent in May as private sector job growth slowed, particularly in several service industries, the government said on Thursday.

The Labor Department said 217,000 overall non-farm jobs were added to payrolls in June, up from 166,000 new jobs in May. But non-government job growth slowed to 151,000 last month from 180,000 in May, it said.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected the report to show the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.8 percent, and an increase of 220,000 in non-farm jobs.

The report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in June, showed that the nation's vibrant labour market did not grow any tighter last month and may have softened slightly in some areas.

On Wednesday, Federal Reserve policy-makers left short-term interest unchanged as indications emerged that the economy was retreating from a torrid 5.9 percent growth rate in the first three months of the year. Many economists believe that growth in the second quarter, which ended on June 30, had slowed to an annual rate of 1.5 percent to 2 percent.
The key manufacturing sector has shown signs of slower growth, with stocks of unsold goods piling up and factory orders having fallen in two of the past three months.
Despite economy's vigour earlier this year, there also have been no signs of a pickup in inflation.
The 217,000 jobs created last month were slightly above the average growth rate of the past year, the department said.
Of the new jobs in June, 66,000 were in government, including 49,000 in local schools, it said.
But the increase could be a statistical fluke, which some economists had expected, as the department's June payroll survey was conducted before the end of the school year.
If that was the case, the absence of the regular annual decline in school employment would have been viewed as a job increase under the department's seasonal adjustment mechanism.

The June payrolls increase included 58,000 new jobs in the retail sector, including 28,000 in bars and restaurants, as well as healthy gains of 11,000 computer and data processing jobs and 14,000 in engineering and management services.
Employment in temporary help services was little changed.
The manufacturing sector added 14,000 jobs in June, up from 5,000 in May.

"Employment gains in manufacturing have been slow but fairly steady since last September, totalling 87,000 over that period," said Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics.

At the same time, factory overtime hours fell by 6 mintues to 4.7 hours per week in June and the factory work week fell by 6 minutes to 41.9 hours, even though both remained near historic high levels.
The department's household survey last month showed the number of job holders falling by 275,000 to 129.36 million, while the number of unemployed workers rose by 302,000 to 6.84 million.
Average hourly earnings last month rose by 4 cents, the same increase as in May, to $12.22, and was up 3.5 percent over the past year, the department said.
